...he makes such mention. And from that poem of Martial he gathers that Pudens the husband — a centurion, or chief centurion, serving in Britain or Germany — was banished into Scotland, beyond the bounds of the Roman empire, on account of his profession of Christian piety: "While it delights you, Aulus, to gaze close at hand upon the Parrhasian Bears and to bear the stars of the Scythian pole."

Here that most ingenious critic conjectures that the word *Scotici* ought to be substituted for *Scythici* — forgetting that in Claudian, Sidonius Apollinaris, and the other ancient writers the first syllable of the name *Scotici* is always read as long, and that in old manuscripts *Scotti* was commonly written everywhere with a doubled letter. Nor is he untrue to form when he adds that Persons "proves, in his treatise on the conversion of England, that Claudia could not have been English" — as though anyone would rave with Dempster's madness so far as to look for England within Britain in Claudia's day, or as though Persons were not striving to establish by his argument that the blessed Claudia whom Paul mentions was not that British woman whose beauty Martial praised under the reign of Trajan, and that she is therefore set up, without any foundation, as either a Scot or an Englishwoman.

And yet that argument on which he chiefly relies, drawn from the reckoning of dates, carries little weight. For even if in the eleventh book of epigrams which I cited there occur some poems written under the third consulship of either Nerva or Trajan, it does not follow that all the rest were composed at the same time. And although the poet died under Trajan, one must nevertheless suppose that he passed away an old man, and that he had earlier been on familiar terms with Silius Italicus, the writer of the Second Punic War.
